q: A bank confirmation reveals a fixed deposit of Rs 5 crore marked as lien in favour of a guarantee issued for a subsidiary. In the financial statements this should be:
o: Shown as restricted other bank balances, with the lien disclosed
Netted off against the guarantee obligation given for the subsidiary
Treated as an investment at fair value through profit or loss
Included within cash and cash equivalents without any comment
why: Deposits under lien are not available for general use and therefore fail the cash equivalents definition, requiring separate presentation and disclosure of the restriction. The related guarantee also needs assessment as a contingent liability or financial guarantee contract.

q: While testing the bank reconciliation, the auditor notes cheques totalling Rs 90 lakh issued on 30 March but despatched to vendors only on 25 April. The most likely conclusion is:
o: A normal outstanding cheque timing difference needing no adjustment
Window dressing understating cash and payables, requiring reversal
A teeming and lading fraud committed on the customer collections
Evidence of an unrecorded bank overdraft at the year end date
why: Cheques recorded as issued but not released to payees do not extinguish the liability, so both cash and trade payables are understated and the current ratio artificially improved. Genuine outstanding cheques are those actually despatched but not yet presented.

q: Teeming and lading is best detected by:
o: Reviewing the fixed deposit register for maturities during the year
Recomputing the bank reconciliation as at the year end date
Comparing receipt dates with banking and customer posting dates
Confirming the year end bank balance directly with each bank
why: Teeming and lading involves delaying the posting of receipts and covering earlier misappropriations with later collections, so lags between receipt, banking and customer posting are the tell-tale sign. A year end bank confirmation shows the total balance and would not reveal the misallocation between customers.

q: A company holds a USD current account. At year end the balance is USD 200000, translated at the closing rate. Under Ind AS 21 the exchange difference on this monetary item is:
o: Adjusted against the cost of the related non-monetary asset
Deferred in equity until the bank account is finally closed
Recognised in other comprehensive income as a translation item
Recognised in profit or loss for the period as it arises
why: Foreign currency bank balances are monetary items retranslated at the closing rate with differences taken to profit or loss. OCI treatment applies to net investment hedges or translation of a foreign operation, not to a routine bank account.

q: The auditor obtains a bank confirmation covering balances but not other arrangements. The most significant gap is:
o: No information on guarantees, liens, security and signatories
No confirmation of the interest rate on the savings account
Failure to obtain a duplicate passbook for the current account
Failure to check the arithmetical accuracy of the statements
why: A standard bank confirmation should also cover contingent liabilities such as guarantees and letters of credit, charges and liens, and signatory details, which are key to completeness of liabilities and disclosure. Balances alone leave off balance sheet exposures untested.

q: During a surprise cash count on 5 April for a 31 March year end, the auditor should:
o: Accept the counted balance as the year end cash on hand
Roll the count back using verified receipts and payments
Ignore the count, since it falls after the balance sheet date
Ask the cashier to reconstruct the 31 March cash position
why: A count after year end is reconciled backwards to the balance sheet date using tested intervening receipts and payments records. Treating the later count as the year end balance ignores all movements in the intervening period.

q: Which item in a bank reconciliation warrants the highest audit scrutiny?
o: Cheques despatched in the last week of March, presented 4 April
Bank charges debited on 31 March and recorded on 2 April
A deposit banked on 31 March but credited only on 20 April
Bank interest credited on 31 March and recorded on 1 April
why: A deposit in transit clearing nearly three weeks later is inconsistent with normal clearing cycles and may indicate a fictitious receipt or receipts recorded early to inflate cash. Small timing differences on charges, interest and recently despatched cheques are routine.

q: A company has a bank overdraft of Rs 2 crore with Bank A and a positive balance of Rs 3 crore with Bank B, without a legal right of set-off. Presentation should be:
o: Rs 2 crore netted from cash with the gross figures disclosed
Both balances presented within cash and cash equivalents
Net cash of Rs 1 crore presented under current assets
Rs 3 crore as cash and bank, Rs 2 crore as a borrowing
why: Offsetting under Ind AS 32 requires a legally enforceable right and intention to settle net, which is absent, so the balances are presented gross. The overdraft is a borrowing under Schedule III unless it forms an integral part of cash management for cash flow statement purposes.

q: The strongest control over payments in a manufacturing company is:
o: Three way matching, dual authorisation and segregated recording
A monthly review of the payment register by the processing clerk
Pre-signed blank cheques held in a locked drawer for urgencies
The accountant who records payments also prepares the cheques
why: Three way matching with dual authorisation and segregation of duties prevents both unauthorised and duplicate payments. Pre-signed cheques and self-review by the preparer are classic control deficiencies that enable misappropriation.

q: A cash flow statement is being audited. A three month fixed deposit taken on 15 February and maturing on 15 May with an original maturity of 90 days, freely encashable, should be:
o: Excluded from cash equivalents because it has a fixed maturity
Included, as original maturity is three months or less
Included only if it matures before the balance sheet date
Shown as an investing outflow at the date it was placed
why: Ind AS 7 treats short term highly liquid investments with an original maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition as cash equivalents. The test runs from acquisition date, not from the balance sheet date.

q: The auditor identifies that the same person receives cash, records it in the cash book and performs the bank reconciliation. The most appropriate audit response is:
o: Test only the year end bank reconciliation in more depth
Offer to prepare the bank reconciliation for the client
Report the deficiency and expand substantive testing
Accept it, as a small company has compensating controls
why: Lack of segregation over the receipt, recording and reconciliation functions creates a serious misappropriation risk that must be communicated and responded to with expanded substantive work. Preparing the reconciliation for the client would impair independence by creating a self-review threat.

q: Kiting, the manipulation of inter-bank transfers around the year end, is most effectively detected by:
o: Recounting the petty cash float held at the head office
Reviewing the interest accrual on the fixed deposits held
Confirming each of the bank balances separately in writing
Preparing a bank transfer schedule around the year end
why: A bank transfer schedule reveals transfers recorded as received before being recorded as paid, or clearing dates straddling the year end, which is precisely how cash is double counted. Individual balance confirmations agree to books that already contain the manipulation.

q: A company reports a large cash balance held at branches abroad in a country with strict exchange controls preventing remittance. The correct treatment is:
o: Include it in cash, disclosing the restriction on its use
Provide fully against the balance as it is not recoverable
Reclassify the amount as an investment in the subsidiary
Exclude the amount from the balance sheet altogether
why: The cash still exists and is controlled by the entity, so it remains recognised, but Ind AS 7 requires disclosure of significant cash balances not available for use by the group. Full provisioning is inappropriate absent evidence of loss of control or impairment.

q: Which procedure primarily addresses completeness of bank accounts rather than accuracy of balances?
o: Recomputing the interest earned on the term deposit account
Reviewing account opening approvals and confirming all banks
Vouching the ten largest payments made during the period
Agreeing the statement balance to the year end reconciliation
why: Reviewing authorisations for account opening and confirming with all banks the entity dealt with during the year detects unrecorded accounts. Procedures starting from recorded accounts cannot identify accounts omitted from the ledger.

q: Cheques on hand at year end that were received from customers on 31 March but banked on 2 April should be:
o: Adjusted only where the amount is material to the current ratio
Excluded from cash and left in receivables until banked
Included in cash on hand, supported by the collection record
Recorded as accrued income until the cheques are cleared
why: Cheques received before the cut-off represent cash on hand and are properly reflected as such, with the customer balance cleared, provided the receipt is substantiated. The auditor tests the collection register and subsequent banking to confirm the receipt date.

q: The auditor notes numerous round sum cash withdrawals described as site expenses with no supporting vouchers, aggregating Rs 40 lakh. The most appropriate response is:
o: Propose a reclassification to miscellaneous site expenses
Reduce the sample size for testing of cash transactions
Accept the explanation, as site operations are cash based
Treat it as a fraud risk indicator and extend procedures
why: Unsupported round sum withdrawals are a classic indicator of misappropriation and require extended procedures and evaluation of the auditor statutory duty to report suspected fraud. Reclassification does not address the underlying occurrence and authorisation risk.

q: A bank confirmation is returned directly to the auditor showing a balance Rs 12 lakh lower than the ledger, and the difference is claimed to be an unrecorded bank charge. The auditor should:
o: Trace the charge and test whether similar items were omitted
Ask the bank to reissue the confirmation with the correction
Ignore it, as the amount is immaterial to the balance sheet
Post the entry without further work, as the bank is external
why: A single unrecorded item may indicate a systematic failure to record bank charges, so projection across the year and control evaluation is necessary. Recording the entry without investigating the cause misses the recurring misstatement.

q: Under Schedule III, cheques and drafts on hand are presented within:
o: Other current assets, alongside prepaid expenses and advances
Cash and cash equivalents, with balances and cash on hand
Other financial assets shown under the non-current heading
Trade receivables, until the instrument is actually realised
why: Schedule III presentation of cash and cash equivalents includes balances with banks, cheques and drafts on hand and cash on hand. Leaving them in receivables would misstate both captions once the instrument has been received.
